title: Is a waterfront city stadium actually on the cards for Canberra?
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Is a waterfront city stadium actually on the cards for Canberra?

A new proposal would place a stadium near the next stage of light rail and within walking distance of the capital's nightlife.

Actual Article Body:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Peter Lusted

Topic:Urban Development and Planning

A bird's-eye view map of the proposed location for an all-event stadium in Canberra's city centre. (Supplied: Canberra Airport)

After it was all but ruled out by the ACT government, a fresh pitch for a city stadium in Canberra has been floated.

The proposal has been met with positive but cautious responses from lawmakers, and although it is likely to be popular among Canberrans, it does not yet have the required land, an owner or a builder.

Here's what's known about the latest pitch for a city stadium.

A new city stadium is being suggested, based on the model of the Te Kaha Stadium in Christchurch — a rectangular stadium with a roof that holds 25,000 fans for sports events and 35,000 for concerts.

That stadium cost about half a billion Australian dollars to deliver.

Canberra's current rectangular stadium in the suburb of Bruce sits in the same precinct as the Australian Institute of Sport, but has drawn criticism in recent years due to its aging infrastructure and location, which means patrons cannot easily stream out to bars and restaurants or public transport.

The proposed site of a new city stadium in Canberra is partially occupied by the Archbishop's House. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The proposed stadium would be waterfront, sitting on the north shore of Lake Burley Griffin near Regatta Place.

The area is a block of Commonwealth land that includes the Catholic Archbishop's house and the car parking next to it.

Crucially, it would be near the next stage of light rail, with construction to take the trams to the lake's edge already underway.

And the proximity to the city would give people the option to walk to Canberra's nightlife after an event.

A consortium of Canberra business heavy-hitters is behind the pitch, including Canberra Airport boss Stephen Byron, the founder of Canberra Data Centres, Greg Boorer, and other corporates.

However, Mr Byron has clarified that the consortium does not want to build the stadium or own it.

That's not yet clear.

The consortium is in discussions with the Catholic Archdiocese to buy the land, and said they would then hand it over for free to whoever runs the project.

That would be either the Commonwealth government, a combination of the Commonwealth and ACT governments, or potentially a private company tasked with developing the stadium.

An artist's rendering of an all-event stadium in Canberra's city (Supplied: Canberra Airport)

The business owners are optimistic the stadium could be complete by 2030.

Their plan is to take six months to get the architect designs finished.

That would then give the ACT government six to 12 months to consider the development and then, if approved, estimate it would take 2.5 years to build.

Canberra's rectangular stadium in Bruce is criticised for its location and age. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The new tram stop would be 80 metres from the proposed stadium.

Mr Byron also said he estimated there were already 7,000 car spaces north and south of the lake, while he said the current Bruce stadium "has about 1,700 car spaces".

He also said he believed that if the lake could fit 120,000 people for Canberra's Skyfire fireworks show, then a live music concert with 35,000 fans, for example, should be fine.

ACT Senator Katy Gallagher did not disagree with the idea of a lakefront stadium. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

ACT Senator Katy Gallagher said the idea was "potentially very exciting" and that the purchase of the Catholic Archbishop's land would be significant.

ACT Treasurer Chris Steel said: "We certainly wouldn't rule out considering this proposal at this stage, we'll see what comes through this new study that's being proposed."

However, he did raise questions about transport to the site, parking and game-day access.
